title: The foundations of cost-sensitive learning
venue: Proceedings of the Seventeenth International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI-01), Seattle, WA. Morgan Kaufmann
harvard_reference: Elkan, C. (2001) 'The foundations of cost-sensitive learning', Proceedings of the Seventeenth International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI-01). Seattle, WA, August 2001. Morgan Kaufmann, pp. 973-978. Available at: https://www.ijcai.org/Proceedings/01/IJCAI-2001-k.pdf (Accessed: 27 September 2026).
abstract_summary: A six-page theoretical paper on optimal decision-making when different misclassification errors carry different costs. Section 1 sets out the decision-theoretic framework: given a cost matrix C(i,j) (cost of predicting class i when the true class is j) and calibrated conditional class probabilities P(j|x), the optimal prediction for x is the class that minimises expected cost, Equation (1). It explains the 'reasonableness' conditions a cost matrix must satisfy, shows that decisions are invariant to scaling and shifting the matrix (so any reasonable two-class matrix can be reduced to a simpler form), warns against economically incoherent matrices, and derives (Section 1.3, Equation (2)) the two-class optimal probability threshold p*, which depends only on the cost-matrix entries and is in general different from 0.5. Section 2 addresses how to make a standard, non-cost-sensitive learner produce decisions at a target threshold p*: the common practice is to rebalance the training set, and Theorem 1 gives the exact multiplier for the number of negative examples (by weighting, oversampling or undersampling), noting that in rare-class domains one should keep all rare-class examples and change only the common class. Section 3 proves Theorem 2, a base-rate correction formula showing how a correct probability estimate changes when the class prior changes (which also allows a classifier trained under one class distribution to be used under another). Section 4 examines what rebalancing actually does to standard learners, explicitly addressing the class-imbalance literature that recommends duplicating or discarding examples so classes are roughly equal (Kubat and Matwin 1997; Japkowicz 2000): for Bayesian learners, changing class frequencies only changes the estimated prior, so there is little reason to expect better decisions at any particular base rate; for naive Bayes, whose probability estimates are poorly calibrated but well ranked, empirically determining an equivalent threshold is likely to improve decisions whereas rebalancing to use a 0.5 threshold is not; for decision-tree growing, the choice of split is invariant to base rates under the Kearns-Mansour criterion (Theorem 3) and only slightly affected under other criteria such as C4.5 entropy; but decision-tree pruning is highly sensitive to class prevalence, so the paper recommends no pruning plus probability smoothing (Laplace) at the leaves. The conclusion (Section 5) is that changing the balance of positive and negative training examples has little effect on these learned classifiers, and that the recommended approach is to learn from the training set as given and then apply Equation (1)/(2) directly to the classifier's probability estimates, smoothing them and/or adjusting the threshold empirically if necessary.

claims_supported.claim: Given calibrated probabilities and a cost matrix, the optimal decision threshold is determined by the cost ratio (threshold moving), so class imbalance is best addressed by adjusting the decision threshold rather than the training data.
claims_supported.where: Supported, with a scope qualification the report should carry. (a) Threshold determined by costs: Section 1 (Equation (1): predict the class with lowest expected cost using P(j|x)) and Section 1.3 'Making optimal decisions' (Equation (2): 'The threshold for making optimal decisions is p* such that ...', with p* a function only of the cost-matrix entries; for the simplified matrix with zero cost for correct predictions this reduces to the ratio of the false-positive cost to the sum of the two error costs, i.e. the cost ratio). The paper's premise is that the probabilities are correct ('probability estimates given by the classifier'; Section 3 assumes estimates 'that we assume are correct given a base rate'); Section 4.1 and the Conclusion add that where estimates are poorly calibrated (naive Bayes) the threshold should be determined empirically or the estimates smoothed - so the 'given calibrated probabilities' precondition is faithful to the paper. Note the paper does not use the phrase 'threshold moving'; that is the report's label. (b) Threshold rather than training data: Abstract and Section 5 Conclusions - 'changing the balance of negative and positive training examples has little effect on the classifiers produced by standard Bayesian and decision tree learning methods. Accordingly, the recommended way ... is to learn a classifier from the training set as given, and then to compute optimal decisions explicitly using the probability estimates given by the classifier'; Section 4 introduction explicitly sets out to test the class-imbalance assumption behind duplicating/discarding examples (Kubat and Matwin 1997; Japkowicz 2000); Section 4.1 last paragraph: empirically choosing an equivalent threshold 'is likely to improve the accuracy of decision-making, while changing the proportion of negative examples using Theorem 1 in order to use the threshold 0.5 is not'; Section 2 (Theorem 1) shows rebalancing is at best a roundabout way of reaching the same threshold p*. SCOPE CAVEAT: the empirical 'little effect' argument is made for standard Bayesian and decision-tree learners (Sections 4.1-4.3), not for all learning algorithms, and Section 4.3 notes decision-tree pruning IS highly sensitive to class prevalence (hence the recommendation to grow unpruned trees with smoothed leaf probabilities). The decision rule of Equations (1)-(2) is general, but 'best addressed' should be attributed as Elkan's recommendation for those learner families, or phrased as the report author's inference.

claims_supported.claim: [Verifier-suggested wording] Elkan (2001) shows that, given a cost matrix and correct class-probability estimates, the cost-minimising decision rule is a fixed probability threshold determined by the misclassification costs (Equation (2)), and argues that rebalancing the training set has little effect on Bayesian and decision-tree classifiers; he therefore recommends training on the data as given and applying the cost-derived threshold (adjusted empirically if the probabilities are poorly calibrated) rather than resampling.
claims_supported.where: Abstract; Section 1.3 (Equation (2)); Section 2 (Theorem 1, rebalancing multiplier); Section 4 introduction and 4.1-4.3; Section 5 Conclusions (learn from the training set as given, then use Equation (1) or (2) directly, 'after smoothing probability estimates and/or adjusting the threshold of Equation (2) empirically if necessary').

caveats: 1) Scope: Elkan's evidence that rebalancing 'has little effect' concerns standard Bayesian (including naive Bayes) and decision-tree learners; the paper makes no empirical claim about logistic regression, gradient boosting or neural networks, although the decision rule in Equations (1)-(2) applies to any classifier producing correct probabilities. Do not cite Elkan as evidence that resampling is useless for every algorithm. 2) Pruning caveat: Section 4.3 states decision-tree pruning is highly sensitive to class prevalence (C4.5 can collapse to a single majority-class node), so the recommendation is unpruned trees with smoothed leaf probabilities - relevant if the report uses tree ensembles. 3) Calibration precondition: the threshold p* is optimal only if the probabilities are correct; Section 4.1 and the Conclusion advise empirical threshold adjustment or smoothing when they are not, so the report should pair this source with a calibration reference when applying it to the Telco data. 4) The phrase 'threshold moving' is not Elkan's terminology. 5) The paper is framed around differing misclassification costs; class imbalance is addressed explicitly only in Section 4 (via Kubat and Matwin 1997 and Japkowicz 2000), so word the citation as a recommendation about handling cost/imbalance at decision time rather than as a study of imbalance per se. 6) No Crossref DOI exists; do not add one. The ACM '10.5555' identifier is not a DOI.
